nameStory: This plant gets its common name "Japanese spikenard" from its native homeland of Japan, where it's called "udo." The "spikenard" part refers to its relationship to other aromatic plants in the Aralia family, whose flowers form distinctive spiky clusters. In Japan, it's also nicknamed "mountain asparagus" because its tender young shoots are harvested and eaten much like asparagus spears.
description: Japanese spikenard is a towering herbaceous perennial that can reach an impressive 6-10 feet tall, making it one of the giants of the understory. This Asian native belongs to the ivy family and produces large, compound leaves and clusters of small flowers followed by dark berries. Unlike woody shrubs, this plant dies back to the ground each winter and sends up fresh shoots each spring. With only one recorded observation in New England, it's an extremely rare find that's likely an escaped garden specimen.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Massive herbaceous plant reaching 6-10 feet tall with thick, sturdy stems that feel smooth and hollow, more like giant celery stalks than woody branches

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very large compound leaves that can span 2-3 feet across, divided into many leaflets with serrated edges that feel papery and smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or greenish flowers arranged in large, branching umbrella-like clusters at the top of the plant, giving off a subtle spicy-sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Young spring shoots are thick and fleshy with a distinctive aromatic smell when broken - pleasantly pungent and slightly bitter, like a cross between celery and ginseng

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small dark purple berries clustered where the flowers were, each about the size of a peppercorn and containing several seeds

habitat: In its native range, Japanese spikenard grows on wooded slopes and forest edges, preferring rich, moist soil with good drainage. In New England, if encountered, it would most likely be found in a cultivated garden setting or possibly escaped near old homesteads where it was grown as an ornamental or food plant.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the ground in late spring, thick and tender - this is when the plant is most easily identified by its distinctive aromatic stems and rapidly expanding compound leaves.
seasonality.summer: Reaches full impressive height with massive leaves and produces its umbrella-like flower clusters in mid to late summer, buzzing with small pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to clusters of dark berries, and leaves begin to yellow and die back, making the plant less conspicuous.
seasonality.winter: Completely dies back to ground level, leaving no above-ground trace except possibly some dried stem remnants.

funFact: In Japan, Japanese spikenard shoots are considered such a delicacy that they're grown in complete darkness in special forcing beds, just like white asparagus, to keep them tender and pale - a single pound of these blanched shoots can sell for over $50 at market!
confusionNotes: Its massive size and compound leaves might remind you of elderberry or other large shrubs, but Japanese spikenard's herbaceous stems (they squish rather than snap like wood) and its ivy-family flower clusters set it apart. Remember: if it's taller than you and feels like a giant herb rather than a woody shrub, you might have found this rarity.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Japanese spikenard," this plant isn't related to the biblical spikenard (which is in the valerian family) - the name simply refers to its aromatic qualities and spiky flower clusters. The confusion around spikenard names has puzzled botanists and herbalists for centuries.
compareHints: Japanese spikenard dwarfs its New England relatives like wild sarsaparilla and American spikenard, growing 2-3 times taller with much more robust stems. While American spikenard might reach 6 feet, it has a more delicate, branching structure, whereas Japanese spikenard grows in massive, thick-stemmed clumps. The leaf arrangement is similar among spikenards, but Japanese spikenard's leaves are notably larger and more substantial.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild sarsaparilla is much shorter than its Aralia relatives - bristly sarsaparilla grows taller with prickly stems, while American spikenard can reach 6 feet with multiple compound leaves and a more robust appearance.

Among New England's Aralia species, bristly sarsaparilla is the shortest and most rough-textured, preferring dry soils unlike wild sarsaparilla's forest preference or American spikenard's love of rich, moist areas.

American spikenard is much larger and more robust than its relatives - wild sarsaparilla stays close to the ground with leaves only 6-12 inches tall, while bristly sarsaparilla is covered in prickles.

Among its Aralia relatives in New England, Japanese angelica tree is by far the tallest and most tree-like, while wild sarsaparilla stays low to the ground and American spikenard is an herbaceous perennial.
Unlike its native New England Aralia cousins which are mostly low woodland herbs, Chinese angelica-tree grows much larger and lacks the thorns found on devil's walkingstick.
Among its Aralia relatives in New England, devil's walkingstick is unmistakable due to its woody, tree-like growth and extensive spines.
